- Final dividend INR 3/share for FY26.

- Capital advances ~INR 906 cr in non-current assets for ongoing capex.
bull_bear.title: Capital Allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **LNG price → volume sensitivity:** High spot prices (war-driven spikes to $25) suppress utilization (March 53%); recovery hinges on prices/conflict.
- **Gulf/Strait of Hormuz geopolitical risk:** Qatar term supply (core ~8.5 mt) halted; resumption depends entirely on conflict resolution. FY27 visibility low; April–May still depressed.
- **Domestic gas competition:** Capacity holders can route cargoes to other Indian terminals (no control over spot mix at Dahej).
- **PDH-PP execution:** Large multi-year capex; equipment sourcing safe but execution/ramp risk remains.
- **Force-majeure / time-charter:** 3 time-charter vessels (Qatar route) idle during disruption; ~INR 90 cr demand for March disputed as FM (company believes not liable).
bull_bear.title: Risks

bull_bear.body: Confident-but-guarded. Repeatedly declined to give FY27 utilization guidance, urging investors to "wait till end of quarter." Optimistic Qatar resumes by June; emphasized record profits and resilience while candid that April–May remain weak ("more or less same as March"). Closing: hopeful Gulf situation improves, "brighter picture" next quarter.
bull_bear.title: Mgmt Tone

bull_bear.body:
- Q4 record profit is materially flattered by the **~INR 495 cr UOP reversal one-off** — underlying operating quarter was hit by the supply shock; FY26 full-year PAT actually fell YoY.
- March Dahej at 53% but Jan–Feb at ~108% shows how concentrated the crisis impact was.
- New Exxon contract is a *portfolio* (Gorgon-sourced) deal, distinct from existing 1.42 mt Exxon contract; Equinor flows via Deepak Fertilizers' Performance Chemiserve.
- National energy-security narrative (CEO press conference) is pivoting Petronet toward strategic storage-tank capex — a new structural growth angle.
- Receivables/payables both fell ~INR 2,000 cr YoY simply because Qatar LNG (and matching RLNG sales) didn't flow in March — optical balance-sheet move, not deterioration.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious

bull_bear.body:
- scale: large regasification terminal with storage that buffers supply disruptions — evidence: Dahej nameplate capacity expanded from 17.5 MMTPA to 22.5 MMTPA in March 2026, operated at 91.9% utilisation in FY 2025-26, with LNG storage of 12,72,000 m³ — against it: MD&A cites 'increasing competition from both existing and upcoming LNG terminals' and steps to optimise capacity bookings at Dahej
- customer lock-in: long-term supply contracts passed through to offtakers on back-to-back terms — evidence: QatarEnergy SPA for 7.5 MMTPA since 2004 offtaken by GAIL, IOCL and BPCL in a 60:30:10 ratio, renewed for another twenty years (2028-2048) with the same offtakers; MARC 1.425 MMTPA contract with back-to-back GSPAs valid till November 2035 — against it: QatarEnergy invoked Force Majeure on 4 March 2026 and Qatar cargoes remained largely disrupted from 3 March 2026
- customer lock-in: multi-year third-party capacity bookings at Dahej — evidence: 5.5-year regasification agreement with Performance Chemiserve for about 25.6 TBTU a year, valid until 31 December 2031
- customer lock-in: long-term ethane handling reservation — evidence: ONGC binding term sheet to reserve about 600 KTPA of ethane handling capacity at the upcoming Dahej USH facilities for 15 years from FY 2028-29 [planned]
- distribution: LNG truck-loading network reaching customers off the pipeline grid — evidence: Dahej loaded a record 13,508 LNG trucks in FY 2025-26 and doubled its truck loading bays from four to eight; Kochi filled 3,236 trucks and doubled its bays from two to four
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Volatility in international LNG prices — Indian demand is price-responsive; consumption in price-sensitive sectors such as fertilizers, power and small industries moderates when LNG prices are high, which hits volumes.
- Geopolitical disruption of LNG supply chains — The West Asia conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption led to force majeure by global suppliers, hurt the company's long-term LNG sourcing, and triggered the Natural Gas (Supply Regulation) Order, 2026, which rationed gas to priority sectors until it was withdrawn on 4 July 2026.
- Competition from existing and upcoming LNG terminals — Management is optimising capacity bookings and throughput at Dahej because of rising terminal competition, which threatens utilisation of the newly expanded capacity.
- Foreign exchange risk, particularly USD-INR — LNG is bought in international markets, so rupee movements affect the business; the company names this as a key risk.
- Delay in gas infrastructure and pipeline connectivity — Slower pipeline build-out limits the demand the terminals can reach and holds back market development.
- Regulatory uncertainty, including delay in GST implementation — Policy and tax uncertainty in the gas sector is named as a key risk to market development and operations.
- Competition from renewable energy and alternate fuels — Substitution by renewables and other fuels could cap growth in natural gas demand.
- Spread between long-term contract prices and spot LNG prices — A wider gap between long-term contract and spot prices may change demand for contracted volumes.

outlook.body:
- Secure long-term LNG supply passed through to offtakers: QatarEnergy SPA for about 7.5 MMTPA renewed for twenty years (delivered basis, 2028-2048) with GAIL, IOCL and BPCL offtaking 60:30:10; ExxonMobil (EMAPPL) SPA of about 1.2 MMTPA for 15 years began supplies in April 2026.
- Grow LNG as a transport fuel for medium and heavy commercial vehicles: four LNG dispensing stations set up in Southern India, a 5th under development at Vallarpadam (Kochi), and more planned along the Delhi-Mumbai and Mumbai-Bangalore highways and in Odisha industrial clusters.
- Expand LNG truck-loading to meet demand from customers off the gas grid: truck loading bays doubled at Dahej (four to eight) and Kochi (two to four).
- Build Kochi into a hub for niche services at one location — gas-up/cool-down (upgraded in 2025), LNG bunkering and LNG reloading, with bunkering and reloading infrastructure being revamped.
- Hold assured shipping capacity for FOB Qatar volumes through three LNG carriers (Disha, Raahi, Aseem) chartered for 25 years each, plus a 3% equity interest in Aseem and a 26% stake in a fourth carrier, Prachi (novated to Exxon Mobil).
- Lift Kochi utilisation through integration with the National Gas Grid once the Coimbatore-Salem-Krishnagiri section of GAIL's KKBMPL pipeline is completed.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Dahej terminal nameplate capacity was expanded from 17.5 MMTPA to 22.5 MMTPA in March 2026. To serve rising demand for LNG delivered by truck, truck loading bays were doubled at Dahej (four to eight) and Kochi (two to four). At Kochi, the gas-up/cool-down facility was upgraded in 2025 and the LNG bunkering and reloading infrastructure is being revamped. Ethane unloading, storage and handling (USH) facilities are upcoming at Dahej, with ONGC reserving about 600 KTPA of capacity for 15 years from FY 2028-29 under a binding term sheet signed on 3 December 2025. A petrochemical project at Dahej is positioned to serve India's polypropylene demand. New third-party contracts back the expanded Dahej capacity: a 5.5-year regasification agreement with Performance Chemiserve (about 25.6 TBTU a year after a 2026 ramp-up, valid to 31 December 2031), a master regasification agreement with ONGC and an RLNG sale master agreement with Mahanagar Gas.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Domestic gas production is projected to see only marginal growth until 2030 as KG-D6 output plateaus and legacy fields decline, so LNG imports are expected to bridge India's demand gap.
- Indian buyers are shifting towards long- and medium-term LNG contracting (around 33 MMTPA of active contracts), which management says improves volume visibility and creates opportunities for more regasification demand at terminals.
- Near-term global LNG market is expected to stay tight and volatile after the Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption, with Europe pulling cargoes to refill low storage and limiting spot availability for Asia.
- Indian LNG demand is price-elastic: consumption in fertilizer and power weakened in FY 2025-26, and price-sensitive markets such as India used demand management during high prices and supply disruptions.
- A liquefaction supply wave from 2027 (North America, Qatar expansions and others) is expected to move the market towards surplus, with excess capacity from around 2029 likely to push LNG prices down.
- City gas distribution demand is rising (RLNG share of India's gas consumption about 51.5% in FY 2025-26), supported by pipeline network expansion to about 27,427 km with another 8,489 km under development.
- India's regasification capacity is expected to rise from 57.7 MMTPA to around 72 MMTPA, adding terminal capacity alongside Petronet's own.
- The market for LNG as a transportation fuel is expected to grow to 8-10 MMTPA over the next 6-8 years.

deepdive.thesis: Quarter dominated by an **ongoing Gulf-region crisis (Strait of Hormuz)** that choked Qatar term-LNG supply from March onward — yet Petronet posted its **highest-ever quarterly PBT (INR 1,795 cr) and PAT (INR 1,338 cr)**, aided by a large Use-of-Pay (UOP) reversal and inventory gains. Dahej ran ~90% for the quarter but collapsed to ~53% in March (vs ~108% Jan–Feb). Mgmt frames the disruption as temporary (Qatar supply resumes 3–4 weeks after conflict ends, hoped by June), with structural offsets: capacity expanded 17.5→22.5 mtpa, two new long-term contracts (Exxon, Equinor ~1 mt combined this year), and a multi-year ~INR 9,000 cr/yr capex cycle led by the PDH-PP petrochem project.

thesis: Quarter dominated by an **ongoing Gulf-region crisis (Strait of Hormuz)** that choked Qatar term-LNG supply from March onward — yet Petronet posted its **highest-ever quarterly PBT (INR 1,795 cr) and PAT (INR 1,338 cr)**, aided by a large Use-of-Pay (UOP) reversal and inventory gains. Dahej ran ~90% for the quarter but collapsed to ~53% in March (vs ~108% Jan–Feb). Mgmt frames the disruption as temporary (Qatar supply resumes 3–4 weeks after conflict ends, hoped by June), with structural offsets: capacity expanded 17.5→22.5 mtpa, two new long-term contracts (Exxon, Equinor ~1 mt combined this year), and a multi-year ~INR 9,000 cr/yr capex cycle led by the PDH-PP petrochem project.

**Use-or-Pay (CALL OUT):** Customers paid INR 630 cr of outstanding UOP dues for CY2022. Net P&L impact INR ~495–496 cr = INR 550 cr CY22 reversal − INR 35 cr (CY23 provision) − INR 6 cr (CY24 provision) − INR 13 cr (volume-linked waiver). **This is a major one-off inflating Q4 profit.**

**Spot-LNG-price → volume effect (CALL OUT):** Post-crisis spot spiked to ~$25/mmbtu (March spot purchases ~$20), now eased to $15–17. Lower prices are reviving utilization vs March; high March prices suppressed volumes.

demand_drivers.body:
- Domestic gas production is projected to see only marginal growth until 2030 as KG-D6 output plateaus and legacy fields decline, so LNG imports are expected to bridge India's demand gap.
- Indian buyers are shifting towards long- and medium-term LNG contracting (around 33 MMTPA of active contracts), which management says improves volume visibility and creates opportunities for more regasification demand at terminals.
- Near-term global LNG market is expected to stay tight and volatile after the Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption, with Europe pulling cargoes to refill low storage and limiting spot availability for Asia.
- Indian LNG demand is price-elastic: consumption in fertilizer and power weakened in FY 2025-26, and price-sensitive markets such as India used demand management during high prices and supply disruptions.
- A liquefaction supply wave from 2027 (North America, Qatar expansions and others) is expected to move the market towards surplus, with excess capacity from around 2029 likely to push LNG prices down.
- City gas distribution demand is rising (RLNG share of India's gas consumption about 51.5% in FY 2025-26), supported by pipeline network expansion to about 27,427 km with another 8,489 km under development.
- India's regasification capacity is expected to rise from 57.7 MMTPA to around 72 MMTPA, adding terminal capacity alongside Petronet's own.
- The market for LNG as a transportation fuel is expected to grow to 8-10 MMTPA over the next 6-8 years.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Dahej terminal nameplate capacity was expanded from 17.5 MMTPA to 22.5 MMTPA in March 2026. To serve rising demand for LNG delivered by truck, truck loading bays were doubled at Dahej (four to eight) and Kochi (two to four). At Kochi, the gas-up/cool-down facility was upgraded in 2025 and the LNG bunkering and reloading infrastructure is being revamped. Ethane unloading, storage and handling (USH) facilities are upcoming at Dahej, with ONGC reserving about 600 KTPA of capacity for 15 years from FY 2028-29 under a binding term sheet signed on 3 December 2025. A petrochemical project at Dahej is positioned to serve India's polypropylene demand. New third-party contracts back the expanded Dahej capacity: a 5.5-year regasification agreement with Performance Chemiserve (about 25.6 TBTU a year after a 2026 ramp-up, valid to 31 December 2031), a master regasification agreement with ONGC and an RLNG sale master agreement with Mahanagar Gas.

management_tone.title: Mgmt Tone
management_tone.body: Confident-but-guarded. Repeatedly declined to give FY27 utilization guidance, urging investors to "wait till end of quarter." Optimistic Qatar resumes by June; emphasized record profits and resilience while candid that April–May remain weak ("more or less same as March"). Closing: hopeful Gulf situation improves, "brighter picture" next quarter.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- scale: large regasification terminal with storage that buffers supply disruptions — evidence: Dahej nameplate capacity expanded from 17.5 MMTPA to 22.5 MMTPA in March 2026, operated at 91.9% utilisation in FY 2025-26, with LNG storage of 12,72,000 m³ — against it: MD&A cites 'increasing competition from both existing and upcoming LNG terminals' and steps to optimise capacity bookings at Dahej
- customer lock-in: long-term supply contracts passed through to offtakers on back-to-back terms — evidence: QatarEnergy SPA for 7.5 MMTPA since 2004 offtaken by GAIL, IOCL and BPCL in a 60:30:10 ratio, renewed for another twenty years (2028-2048) with the same offtakers; MARC 1.425 MMTPA contract with back-to-back GSPAs valid till November 2035 — against it: QatarEnergy invoked Force Majeure on 4 March 2026 and Qatar cargoes remained largely disrupted from 3 March 2026
- customer lock-in: multi-year third-party capacity bookings at Dahej — evidence: 5.5-year regasification agreement with Performance Chemiserve for about 25.6 TBTU a year, valid until 31 December 2031
- customer lock-in: long-term ethane handling reservation — evidence: ONGC binding term sheet to reserve about 600 KTPA of ethane handling capacity at the upcoming Dahej USH facilities for 15 years from FY 2028-29 [planned]
- distribution: LNG truck-loading network reaching customers off the pipeline grid — evidence: Dahej loaded a record 13,508 LNG trucks in FY 2025-26 and doubled its truck loading bays from four to eight; Kochi filled 3,236 trucks and doubled its bays from two to four

risks.title: Risks
risks.body:
- **LNG price → volume sensitivity:** High spot prices (war-driven spikes to $25) suppress utilization (March 53%); recovery hinges on prices/conflict.
- **Gulf/Strait of Hormuz geopolitical risk:** Qatar term supply (core ~8.5 mt) halted; resumption depends entirely on conflict resolution. FY27 visibility low; April–May still depressed.
- **Domestic gas competition:** Capacity holders can route cargoes to other Indian terminals (no control over spot mix at Dahej).
- **PDH-PP execution:** Large multi-year capex; equipment sourcing safe but execution/ramp risk remains.
- **Force-majeure / time-charter:** 3 time-charter vessels (Qatar route) idle during disruption; ~INR 90 cr demand for March disputed as FM (company believes not liable).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious
non_obvious.body:
- Q4 record profit is materially flattered by the **~INR 495 cr UOP reversal one-off** — underlying operating quarter was hit by the supply shock; FY26 full-year PAT actually fell YoY.
- March Dahej at 53% but Jan–Feb at ~108% shows how concentrated the crisis impact was.
- New Exxon contract is a *portfolio* (Gorgon-sourced) deal, distinct from existing 1.42 mt Exxon contract; Equinor flows via Deepak Fertilizers' Performance Chemiserve.
- National energy-security narrative (CEO press conference) is pivoting Petronet toward strategic storage-tank capex — a new structural growth angle.
- Receivables/payables both fell ~INR 2,000 cr YoY simply because Qatar LNG (and matching RLNG sales) didn't flow in March — optical balance-sheet move, not deterioration.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Secure long-term LNG supply passed through to offtakers: QatarEnergy SPA for about 7.5 MMTPA renewed for twenty years (delivered basis, 2028-2048) with GAIL, IOCL and BPCL offtaking 60:30:10; ExxonMobil (EMAPPL) SPA of about 1.2 MMTPA for 15 years began supplies in April 2026.
- Grow LNG as a transport fuel for medium and heavy commercial vehicles: four LNG dispensing stations set up in Southern India, a 5th under development at Vallarpadam (Kochi), and more planned along the Delhi-Mumbai and Mumbai-Bangalore highways and in Odisha industrial clusters.
- Expand LNG truck-loading to meet demand …

challenges.title: Challenges → Beneficiaries
challenges.body:
- Gulf supply disruption → spot/portfolio LNG players (Golden Pass/US, Oman, Mozambique, Nigeria, Congo, Mauritania/Senegal) and capacity holders (GAIL, IOCL, BPCL, GSPC) diverting cargoes. ⭐
- National storage-shortfall concern → terminal/storage-tank EPC and Petronet's own tank build-out (Gopalpur, Kochi, Dahej). ✅

thesis: Quarter dominated by an **ongoing Gulf-region crisis (Strait of Hormuz)** that choked Qatar term-LNG supply from March onward — yet Petronet posted its **highest-ever quarterly PBT (INR 1,795 cr) and PAT (INR 1,338 cr)**, aided by a large Use-of-Pay (UOP) reversal and inventory gains. Dahej ran ~90% for the quarter but collapsed to ~53% in March (vs ~108% Jan–Feb). Mgmt frames the disruption as temporary (Qatar supply resumes 3–4 weeks after conflict ends, hoped by June), with structural offsets: capacity expanded 17.5→22.5 mtpa, two new long-term contracts (Exxon, Equinor ~1 mt combined this year), and a multi-year ~INR 9,000 cr/yr capex cycle led by the PDH-PP petrochem project.

**Use-or-Pay (CALL OUT):** Customers paid INR 630 cr of outstanding UOP dues for CY2022. Net P&L impact INR ~495–496 cr = INR 550 cr CY22 reversal − INR 35 cr (CY23 provision) − INR 6 cr (CY24 provision) − INR 13 cr (volume-linked waiver). **This is a major one-off inflating Q4 profit.**

**Spot-LNG-price → volume effect (CALL OUT):** Post-crisis spot spiked to ~$25/mmbtu (March spot purchases ~$20), now eased to $15–17. Lower prices are reviving utilization vs March; high March prices suppressed volumes.

**Other one-offs:** Inventory gain INR 95 cr; trading gains INR 118 cr; IndAS Q4 gross-margin +INR 119 cr (FY +629 cr), Q4 FOREX loss INR 91 cr (FY −199 cr).

- **Volume/utilization outlook:** Refused a firm FY27 number given Gulf uncertainty. April–May utilization "more or less at the same level as March" (~53% Dahej). Hopeful Qatar supply resumes from **first week of June** (3–4 weeks after conflict ends), reverting to annual delivery plan; talking to Qatar to make good lost volumes within FY27.
- **Tariff hike:** **Kochi regas tariff +5% from April 2026** (constant escalation).
- **PDH-PP / Petchem:** Project "absolutely on track"; equipment sourced from Japan/Korea/China/Europe/US (not Gulf), so unaffected. ~INR 1,650 cr spent in FY26; ~INR 7,500 cr (±10%) budgeted FY27 — the bulk of capex.
- **Capex:** **FY27 ~INR 9,000 cr** (cash basis lower; FY26 cash capex was INR 2,511 cr vs INR 3,000 cr provisioned). FY28 also ~INR 9,000 cr (±10%).
- **New terminals:** Gopalpur terminal construction to start FY27 (~INR 300–400 cr this year, 2 tanks). Third jetty at Dahej (~INR 600 cr). Fifth small-scale LNG plant at Kochi (~INR 70 cr, land acquired).

themes.title: Oil & Gas - gas economy (CGD/LNG) + refining/upstream
themes.need: India's gas-economy push now collides with an outright policy reversal. ATGL grew volume 13% to 303 MMSCM and revenue 27% to INR 1,908cr, yet EBITDA FELL sequentially to INR 281cr (~14.7% margin, from INR 310cr) because the government withdrew the pooled-gas mechanism after the West Asia 'peace deal', pushing ATGL to ~15% spot volumes with Brent above $107/bbl; management also noted NWG price is 12% of the Indian crude basket, so a 62% domestic mix protects far less than it looks, and CNG station adds slowed to +5 from +25 in Q4 even as CNG demand grows ~30%. The same shock ran the other way for integrated refining: RELIANCE delivered O2C EBITDA of INR 17,000cr (+17%) THROUGH the Strait-of-Hormuz closure at 96-97% throughput while Asian peers ran 15-20% below capacity, with ethane+ROGC at ~70% of ethylene feed as distillate cracks blew out (gas oil $16 to $63, ATF $14 to $62). MGL/GUJGASLTD/IGL/IRMENERGY carry the same CGD margin squeeze; PETRONET/OIL/ONGC/IOC ride LNG-infra + domestic-gas; CHENNPETRO/MRPL ride GRM cracks; DEEPINDS/JINDRILL/SEAMECLTD on ONGC E&P capex; AEGISLOG/AEGISVOPAK add LPG/gas terminalling.
themes.driver: Whether the pooled/APM gas-allocation mechanism is restored (the single biggest CGD earnings variable); LNG spot price and Brent; GRM/distillate cracks; ONGC rig tenders & day-rates.
